content: The use of antiseptic solutions prior to cesarean sections has been studied to evaluate their effectiveness in preventing postoperative infections. A Cochrane review from 2014 assessed the quality of evidence and outcomes related to various antiseptic agents and methods of application. 1. Antiseptic Agents for Preoperative Skin Preparation: Alcohol scrub plus iodophor drape vs. iodophor scrub alone: The evidence quality was rated as low, with a small sample size and few events reported. The confidence interval crossed the line of no effect, indicating uncertainty in the results. Chlorhexidine gluconate vs. povidone-iodine: The evidence quality was very low, with one study showing design limitations, a small sample size, and few events. The results suggested fewer infections per 1,000 patients, but the wide confidence interval limits the reliability of this finding. Parachlorometaxylenol plus iodine vs. iodine alone: The evidence quality was low, with wide confidence intervals and a small sample size. The results were inconclusive due to the limited data. 2. Method of Application of Antiseptic Agents: Drape vs. no drape: The evidence quality was moderate, but the studies contributing to the pooled effect had design limitations. The confidence interval crossed the line of no effect, indicating uncertainty in the benefit of using a drape. Alcohol with drape vs. iodophor without drape: The evidence quality was low, with small sample sizes and no events reported in some studies. The results were inconclusive. 3. Prophylactic Antibiotics for Cesarean Sections: Any antibiotic vs. no prophylaxis: The evidence quality was moderate, with most studies showing design limitations. Antibiotics reduced infections by 28 per 1,000 patients. By class of antibiotics: The evidence quality varied from moderate to very low. For example: First-generation cephalosporins vs. penicillins: Very low-quality evidence with no significant difference in outcomes. Second-generation cephalosporins vs. penicillins: Low-quality evidence with wide confidence intervals and few events. Fluoroquinolones vs. penicillins: Very low-quality evidence with design limitations and small sample sizes. 4. Timing of Prophylactic Antibiotics: Administering antibiotics before skin incision was associated with fewer infections compared to administration after cord clamping. The evidence quality was high, with a reduction of 16 infections per 1,000 patients. 5. Maternal Adverse Effects: Studies on maternal allergic reactions, nausea, vomiting, and skin rash showed very low-quality evidence. Most studies had small sample sizes, few events, and design limitations, making it difficult to draw reliable conclusions. 6. Comparison of Antibiotic Classes: Third-generation cephalosporins vs. penicillins: Very low-quality evidence with no significant difference in outcomes. Fluoroquinolones vs. cephalosporins: Very low-quality evidence with wide confidence intervals and few events. Lincosamide/aminoglycoside vs. penicillins: Very low-quality evidence with inconclusive results. In summary, while some interventions, such as the timing of prophylactic antibiotics, show clear benefits, the evidence for other comparisons remains limited due to small sample sizes, design limitations, and wide confidence intervals. Further high-quality research is needed to provide more definitive guidance on the prevention and treatment of maternal peripartum infections.
